claim: Amazon's commingling program allowed counterfeit supplements to mix with genuine products in the same warehouse bin, enabling consumers to receive fakes even when buying directly from a brand's official Amazon storefront; Amazon announced shutdown by mid-2026.
scope_conditions: Amazon marketplace, global, prior to mid-2026
quoted_support: Amazon would pool 'identical' products from multiple sellers into the same warehouse bin... Even if you bought directly from the brand's Amazon storefront, you could get a fake. Amazon announced they're shutting down their 'commingling' program by mid-2026.

claim: Research on 121 supplement products found 5% exceeded safe daily arsenic limits, 2% had excess lead, cadmium, and aluminum, and 1% contained excess mercury — levels high enough to cause cognitive impairment, brittle bones, dementia, or cancer.
scope_conditions: Supplement products analyzed in research study
quoted_support: Research analyzing 121 supplement products found alarming contamination rates: 5% exceeded safe daily limits for arsenic, 2% had excess lead, cadmium, and aluminum, 1% contained too much mercury.

claim: A study of 12 prenatal multivitamins found 11 of 12 had at least one nutrient outside acceptable deviation from label claims — including folic acid, iodine, iron, and vitamins A, C, and E critical for fetal development.
quoted_support: 11 of 12 prenatal multivitamins had at least one tested nutrient outside the acceptable deviation from what the label claimed. Folic acid, iodine, iron, vitamins A, C, and E (all critical for fetal development) were either under-dosed or over-dosed compared to label claims.

claim: Research on herbal supplements found 16 of 40 tested products contained pesticide residues that appeared to exceed legal limits.
stance_target: Herbal supplement safety and regulatory compliance
quoted_support: Research on herbal supplements found that 16 of 40 supplements tested contained pesticide residues that appeared to exceed legal limits.

claim: GMP certification applies to the manufacturing facility, not individual products — a GMP-certified facility can produce poor-quality supplements if procedures are not followed or corners are cut.
stance_target: GMP certification as product-level quality guarantee
quoted_support: GMP certification applies to the facility, not individual products. A GMP-certified facility can produce high-quality supplements. But they could also produce poor-quality ones if they're not following their own procedures, cutting corners, or working with substandard ingredients. GMP certification is table stakes.

claim: 'FDA-registered facility' means only that the facility registered its existence with the FDA — it is a mandatory compliance requirement, not an achievement or endorsement. Supplements claiming 'FDA-approved' are either confused or lying.
quoted_support: 'FDA-registered facility' means the facility told the FDA it exists. That's it... If a supplement claims FDA approval, they're either confused or lying.

claim: A Certificate of Analysis (COA) is only meaningful when it matches the specific batch/lot number on the consumer's bottle — a COA for a different batch is irrelevant to the product in hand.
quoted_support: You need to verify the COA matches your actual product. If a brand shows you a COA but it's for a different batch number than what you have, that COA is irrelevant to your product. Each batch needs its own testing.

claim: Third-party certifications (USP, NSF, ConsumerLab) are voluntary and costly, meaning a high-quality supplement without third-party certification may still be well-manufactured — absence of certification is not automatically a quality red flag.
stance_target: Third-party supplement certifications as mandatory quality requirement
quoted_support: These certifications are voluntary and costly. A supplement can be high-quality, properly manufactured, and contain exactly what it claims and still not have third-party certification, simply because the manufacturer hasn't paid for the testing and audit process.

claim: DNA sequencing studies have found herbal supplements claiming to contain specific herbs that actually contain completely different plants, with expensive herbs replaced by cheap fillers or active ingredients missing entirely.
quoted_support: Studies using DNA sequencing have found supplements claiming to contain specific herbs that actually contained completely different plants. In some cases, expensive herbs were replaced with cheap fillers. In others, the active ingredient was missing entirely.
